summary: The note surveys how cities use data analytics, apps, and new design approaches to make urban parks more accessible and useful. It covers sensor-driven planning, community apps, pocket parks, brownfield conversion, edible rooftop gardens, inclusive playground design, green transport corridors, and citizen science. Each strategy is illustrated with a named project, location, launch date, and a quote from the person leading it.
one_line: Cities are using data, apps, pocket parks, brownfield reuse, inclusive design, green corridors, and citizen science to improve access to urban parks.
key_facts: Smart sensors and IoT devices installed in parks since September 2023 provide data on peak usage times, popular areas, and foot traffic flow.
Urban planner Johnathon Andrews said on November 5th, 2023 that real-time data helps design green spaces that are more welcoming and align with community needs.
Tech start-up GreenGo launched a park app in Chicago on January 15, 2024, using geolocation to guide visitors through nature trails and historical tours.
As of October 2023, Seattle's ParkVoice app has been used to gather community feedback on proposed park projects.
New York City's Green Patches Initiative, led by urban planner Susan Chen, began September 27th, 2023 and aims to turn overlooked city nooks into green spots by 2025.

Bluebell Fields in Detroit, a former automobile manufacturing plant, opened as a park on April 22nd, 2024 (Earth Day), led by environmental engineer Marcus Lei using soil remediation and sustainable landscaping.
Gardens in the Sky, launched in San Francisco on September 12th, 2023, turns rooftops into communal vegetable gardens to combat food deserts; project coordinator is Amy Wellington.
Central Park's southern playground redesign, completed December 5th, 2023, added sensory gardens for neurodivergent children and adults and wheelchair-accessible pathways.
Playground designer Elena Rodriguez said the redesign is about offering equal access to nature irrespective of ability or background.
New York unveiled its Emerald Links green corridor initiative on August 21st, 2024, following Amsterdam's Green Veins project, which connects suburban areas to city parks via cycling paths.
Urban cycling advocate Pedro Gomez said Emerald Links is about engaging New Yorkers with their city's green lungs through healthy transit options.
London's Urban Nature Watch citizen science program launched March 14th, 2024, with wildlife biologist Emma Thompson overseeing tracking of wildlife and plant health in public parks.
